questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presented with rectal prolapse. He had arrived in the UK 2 weeks earlier. He was normally resident in Vietnam. He reported recurrent intermittent episodes of mild abdominal pain for as long as he can remember. On examination he appeared small in stature, but otherwise the exam was unremarkable. Feces microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely infective cause?
questions.explanation: Trichuris trichiura The most likely organism here is Trichuris trichiura. Rectal prolapse is a known complication of this infection. Trichuris ova are typically 50 × 20 μm in size and are barrel-shaped. They have a smooth wall with a hyaline plug at both ends. Egg numbers usually correlate with adult worm burden. (Image from Bogitsh B, Carter C, Oeltman T , eds. Human Parasitology. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2019.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q33

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented with acute breathlessness, wheeze, and severe abdominal pain. He had a past medical history of allergic rhinitis which he controlled with antihistamines as required. One week earlier he had been diagnosed with temporal arteritis for which he started a course of high-dose oral prednisolone. He denied excessive alcohol use, smoking, or consuming any illicit drug use. He lived in Peru until age 18 years when he emigrated to the UK for work. On examination the patient was unwell. Vitals revealed respiratory rate 28 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 92% on 15 L/minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, heart rate 124 beats/minute, and temperature 38.5°C. He had a diffuse wheeze throughout his chest and was unable to complete sentences. He had generalized abdominal pain with no guarding and normal bowel sounds. Initial investigations: Hemoglobin: 132 g/L (135–180) Total WCC: 20.8 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) (neutrophils 15.2, lymphocytes 1.5, monocytes 1.1) Platelets: 178 ×109/L (150–450) Urea: 9.2 mmol/L (2.8–8.1) Creatinine: 112 μmol/L (62–106) Amylase: 1250 U/L (60–180) Cholesterol and triglycerides were normal Urgent chest X-ray: Urgent abdominal USS revealed sludge in a normal gallbladder but no gallstones or blockage of common bile or cystic duct.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfestation Strongyloides hyperinfestation is the most likely condition. Strongyloides are nematodes (roundworms) that may be acquired from dogs and other companion animals, but also from soil or other materials contaminated with human feces. Countries in South America (particularly Peru) have a high prevalence of Strongyloides infection, and consequently latent asymptomatic infection is common. Hyperinfestation illness can occur in patients with underlying asymptomatic disease who become immunosuppressed, as in this case with high-dose steroids. Consider asking patients about clinical manifestations of initial infection (rash, respiratory symptoms). Strongyloides-associated pancreatitis is a recognized feature of hyperinfestation illness but remains an infrequent cause of acute pancreatitis, particularly in immunocompetent hosts. The patient’s total leucocyte count and neutrophil count is raised. Neutrophilia commonly reflects bacterial infection, but it should be noted that steroids cause an accelerated release of neutrophils from the bone marrow. As a result neutrophilia is commonly seen in patients receiving steroid therapy. In this scenario the total leucocyte count is not completely accounted for by neutrophils, lymphocytes, or monocytes. This suggests that another leucocyte is raised, such as eosinophils, which would fit with tissue-migratory helminth infection. Acute cholangitis is a common condition although the patient does not have classic risk factors, clinical features, or radiologic findings. Of note, the absence of gallstones or inflammation on USS does not entirely rule this out but does make this condition less likely. The chest X-ray reveals bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which are seen in SIRS, but can also be seen in other conditions including atypical pneumonia and hyperinfestation illness. Community-acquired pneumonia caused by mycoplasma can present as severe shortness of breath with extrapulmonary features such as pancreatitis. Despite this, the clinical situation is atypical for mycoplasma infection as it is most common in patients <40 years old, symptoms crescendo over 2–3weeks, and are commonly associated with cough and headaches (absent in the patient). Blood tests can also reveal a hemolytic anemia (again absent). Adult-onset asthma is plausible, particularly as he has a history of atopy, but this is uncommon, and the association of other features (pancreatitis) makes this unlikely. Acute HIV classically presents as an infectious mononucleosis-type illness with fever, rash, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. Atypical presentations with involvement of different body systems can occur but as the patient does not have clear risk factors (although these should be clarified) and lymphocyte count is normal, this would make acute HIV unlikely. An HIV test should still be performed. (Image from Wang Y, Ma Y, Xu Y, et al. Strongyloides stercoralis disseminated infection in a patient misdiagnosed with chronic asthmatic bronchitis. J Microbiol Immunol Infect. 2016;49(1):154–156.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q17

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man was reviewed with longstanding generalized abdominal pain. He had moved to the UK 4 years previously from Uganda where he had been born and brought up. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL MCV 69 fL Eosinophil count 0.5 ×109/L Feces microscopy for ova, cysts, and parasites ×1: negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Albendazole The history of chronic abdominal pain, microcytic anemia, mild eosinophilia, and epidemiologic exposure is most likely to be explained by a hookworm infection. Albendazole (or mebendazole) is used most frequently as first-line treatment. Iron replacements may be used, but anemia will recur without specific treatment to clear the parasites. Pyrantel is a good alternative; ivermectin has poor activity against hookworm. There is no indication for DEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q32

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man was reviewed for ongoing epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He had been born and brought up in Thailand and had moved to the United States age 18. Investigation: Peripheral eosinophil count 1.4 ×109/L Stool OCP ×3 negative Strongyloides serology positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin While both ivermectin and albendazole have activity against Strongyloides, ivermectin has a better reported efficacy. Pentamidine, praziquantel, and suramin have no role in the treatment of strongyloidiasis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q9

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. She had received a deceased donor kidney transplant for polycystic kidney disease 3 months prior. She had received antithymocyte globulin for induction and was on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. She rapidly developed a purpuric rash and respiratory failure and required intubation. Gross hematuria was seen on urinary catheterization. Bronchoscopy: diffuse hemorrhage seen. She was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
questions.lead_in: In addition to supportive critical care, what is the best therapeutic intervention?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin per NG The patient has Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome. Light microscopy of urine showed larvae consistent with Strongyloides.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q41

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of an itchy rash on her leg. She had returned 2 weeks earlier from a holiday in the Caribbean. On exam:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous larva migrans The rash is characteristic and diagnostic of cutaneous larva migrans (CLM), pruritic, serpiginous, located in lower extremities. CLM is a result of infection by animal hookworm larvae, most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense or A. caninum. These are found worldwide, but infection is commoner in tropical and subtropical regions. The larvae can penetrate the skin but cannot pass through the basement membrane of the epidermis. They migrate slowly at a few centimeters/day, causing an inflammatory response along their track. This manifests as an intensely pruritic, red, raised, serpiginous lesion, usually on a lower extremity, or any part of the body exposed to contaminated sand. The actual larvae are a centimeter or two ahead of the lesion. Lesions normally resolve within 2–8 weeks. Gnathostomiasis can cause localized lesions, but these are associated with edema and pain as well as itching and erythema. Most cases are reported from Asia (especially Thailand and Japan) as well as Mexico. Larva currens is caused by infection with Strongyloides stercoralis. It is also a serpiginous eruption, but the tracks are less defined. They are much faster moving than CLM lesions, at approximately 5 cm/hour, but only last a few hours. Phytophotodermatitis is caused by topical exposure to certain plant substances; commonly lime juice. Irregular itchy blisters and erythematous patches develop on sunexposed skin. Linear lesions are common. Lesions appear 24 hours after sun exposure, are not pruritic, but may be painful. (Image from Kincaid L, Klowak M, Klowak S, Boggild AK. Management of imported cutaneous larva migrans: a case series and mini-review. Travel Med Infect Dis. 2015;13(5):382–387.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q47

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy was reviewed with a 4-week history of mild abdominal discomfort, anorexia, and some loose stools. He was normally resident in California but had returned from 2 months living with family in Mexico 1 month prior to symptom onset. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Stool OCP:
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be causing his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides The egg seen is that of Ascaris lumbricoides. Stool OCP (ova, cysts, and parasites) microscopy is usually positive in Ascaris infection due to the huge numbers of eggs that are produced and shed. Fertilized eggs are rounded with a thick bumpy outer shell, often stained brown. Abdominal symptoms are often absent or nonspecific unless an adult worm is passed in the stool. It takes around 6–8 weeks after egg ingestion for abdominal symptoms to develop. (Image from Maguire JH. Intestinal nematodes (roundworms). In Bennett JE, Dolin R, Blaser MJ, eds. Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett’s Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases. Updated 8th ed. Elsevier; 2015.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q29

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl was reviewed with nausea and epigastric pain made worse on eating. There was no diarrhea. She had no other medical problems and did not take any regular medications. She was normally resident in Florida but had recently returned from a 3-month stay in Costa Rica with family. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations: Absolute eosinophil count 0.6 ×109/L Stool microscopy:
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be causing her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Necator americanus This is a hookworm egg. It is not possible to distinguish between Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus on microscopy (that requires the larval stage), but geographically this is more likely to be Necator americanus. (Image from Maguire JH. Intestinal nematodes (roundworms). In Bennett JE, Dolin R, Blaser MJ, eds. Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett’s Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases. Updated 8th ed. Elsevier; 2015.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q29

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman from Jamaica has a history of chronic, watery diarrhea. Recently, she had to receive highdose steroids for a new diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. She presents now with several days of fever and headache, and her blood cultures and CSF cultures are growing Escherichia coli.
questions.lead_in: In addition to antibacterial therapy, what additional medications could be considered to treat her underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin This patient likely has infection with Strongyloides stercoralis, which is more common in tropical countries. It typically causes infection limited to the lung and GI tract, but, in immunocompromised hosts, it can also cause hyperinfection syndrome that can present as gram-negative bacteremia and meningitis because of parasite-driven translocation of enteric bacteria. Treatment of choice for strongyloidiasis is ivermectin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q40

questions.question: Pinworm question – kid been treated multiple times, brother symptomatic, treated once, parents asymptomatic, never been treated

parts.text: Org that causes pinworms?
What are 2 management recommendations?
How should you deal with the laundry? Be specific about what you would wash and how.
What 2 non-drug measures can you advice the family?

questions.model_answer:
a) Organism: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm).
b) Management: (1) treat the entire household simultaneously, not just symptomatic members, with albendazole 400 mg (or mebendazole 100 mg) single dose, repeated in 2 weeks (2) treat asymptomatic household contacts too, since asymptomatic carriage is common and untreated contacts perpetuate reinfection.
c) Laundry: on the day treatment starts, wash all bedding, pajamas, and underwear in hot water and dry on a hot cycle; avoid shaking linens before washing (this aerosolizes eggs).
d) Non-drug measures: (1) trim fingernails short and discourage nail-biting/scratching (2) morning bathing/showering and hand hygiene before meals to reduce autoinfection and environmental egg spread.

questions.question: Nematode, cestode, trematode? and treatment

parts.text: Trichuris tricuria
Strongyloides stercoralis
Diphyllobothrium latum
Schisto
Fasiocola hepatica

questions.model_answer:
Trichuris trichiura - nematode; treatment: albendazole 400 mg daily for 3 days (or mebendazole 500 mg x3 days), sometimes combined with ivermectin for heavy infection.
Strongyloides stercoralis - nematode; treatment: ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day for 2 days.
Diphyllobothrium latum - cestode; treatment: praziquantel (single dose).
Schistosoma species - trematode; treatment: praziquantel.
Fasciola hepatica - trematode; treatment: triclabendazole (praziquantel is NOT effective against Fasciola).
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3437-3441 (nematodes); other classes beyond this chapter
questions.beyond_mandell: Cestode/trematode treatment (Diphyllobothrium, Schistosoma, Fasciola) from standard parasitology references, not this nematode chapter.

questions.question: Recurrent Pinworm infection in an 8 year old boy. Responds to treatment but symptoms return. Brother also had it recently – (2019)

parts.text: What is the organism?
What is important about medication administration for this family?
What should be laundered and how? (only a single line provided for the answer)
Other than laundry and avoiding butt scratching what are TWO non-medication things this family should do?

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Enterobius vermicularis. Medication: Simultaneous treatment of the entire household is warranted regardless of symptoms; Albendazole 400mg PO once, repeat in 2 weeks. Laundry: All beddings and clothes should be washed in high heat (ideally in AM because eggs get laid at night). Other measures: Frequent handwashing; Shower (avoid baths); Clipping of fingernails

questions.question: Geohelminths - indicate if the listed helminth is a nematode (round), cestode (tape), or trematode (flat) and the first line treatment for each – (2019)

parts.text: Strongyloides stercoralis | Type of helminth | First line Tx
Schistosoma mansoni | Type of helminth | First line Tx
Trichuris trichiura | Type of helminth | First line Tx
Fasciola hepatica | Type of helminth | First line Tx
Diphyllobothrium latum | Type of helminth | First line Tx

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides stercoralis - Nematode - Ivermectin. Schistosoma mansoni - Trematode - Praziquantel. Trichuris trichiura - Nematode - Mebendazole. Fasciola hepatica - Trematode - Triclabendazole. Diphyllobothrium latum - Cestode - Albendazole

questions.question: 27. Child went to South America. Asymptomatic. Had stool O+P.

parts.text: Do you treat and if yes, what drug: Blastocystis hominis / E. hartmanni / Trichuris trichiura / Strongyloides stercoralis
Sibling travelled, had abdo pain and stool O+P shows E. histolytica/dispar. What one test do you suggest and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) Treatment decisions: Blastocystis hominis - do not treat (nonpathogenic/commensal in an asymptomatic patient). E. hartmanni - do not treat (nonpathogenic commensal ameba). Trichuris trichiura - treat even if asymptomatic: albendazole 400 mg daily x3 days (or mebendazole). Strongyloides stercoralis - always treat, even if asymptomatic, due to risk of autoinfection/hyperinfection: ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day x2 days.
b) Sibling with abdominal pain and E. histolytica/dispar on stool O&P: order a stool E. histolytica-specific antigen test (or PCR), because microscopy cannot distinguish pathogenic E. histolytica from the morphologically identical, nonpathogenic E. dispar - only confirmed E. histolytica requires treatment.

questions.question: 25yo F, previously healthy returning from S. America with diarrhea x several weeks but now asymptomatic. Had stool O+P showing the following, do you treat and if yes, what drug: Blastocystis hominis / E. hartmannii / Trichuris trichiura / Strongyloides stercoralis

parts.text: Do you treat and if yes, what drug, for each of: Blastocystis hominis; E. hartmannii; Trichuris trichiura; Strongyloides stercoralis
Boyfriend also travelled with her, had abdo pain and stool O+P shows E. histolytica/dispar. What one test do you suggest and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) Blastocystis hominis - no treatment (nonpathogenic commensal, patient asymptomatic). E. hartmannii - no treatment (nonpathogenic). Trichuris trichiura - treat regardless of symptoms: albendazole 400 mg daily x3 days. Strongyloides stercoralis - always treat: ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day x2 days (risk of hyperinfection if untreated).
b) Boyfriend with abdominal pain and E. histolytica/dispar on stool: send a stool antigen test (or PCR) specific for E. histolytica, since microscopy alone cannot differentiate pathogenic E. histolytica from nonpathogenic E. dispar, and only E. histolytica warrants antiparasitic treatment.

questions.question: Geohelminths = major soil-transmitted intestinal nematodes that cause human diseases

parts.text: a) Aside from Strongyloides, name 3 other organisms.
b) What are 2 public health concerns they raise in endemic settings
c) Name two public health strategies for controlling them.
d) What syndrome in developed countries/non-endemic regions related to them?

cohort_answer.text: a) Hookworm (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale); Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura. b) Anemia; Vitamin/nutrient deficiency in children; Secondary neurologic complications from nutritional deficiency; Dehydration. c) Treatment of potential hosts (dogs, cats); Mass anthelmintic treatment; Sanitation/Sewage control; Shoes; education. d) Loeffler's syndrome; Strongyloides Hyperinfection.

questions.question: Strongyloides with filiaria co-infection

parts.text: a) What is the risk of ivermectin?
b) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for Strongy going to start immunosuppression

cohort_answer.text: a) If heavy Loa loa infection, ivermectin can precipitate an encephalopathy (mechanism unknown, believed related to high microfilaremia and rapid killing of worms - Mazzotti reaction); pre-treat with Albendazole. b) Screen with stool and serology (high sens, low specificity, positive with Wuchereria, Brugia, Onchocerca, Mansonella); Treat empirically with Albendazole or apheresis.

questions.question: 9.  Photo showing cutaneous larva migrans

parts.text: A.  What are two causative organisms? Both genus and species names are required.
B.  The gp wants to know if they have to worry about systemic disease.  Yes or no and why?
C. What is the treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
a) Dog/cat hookworm: Ancylostoma brasiliensis and Ancylostoma caninum. Human Hookworm: Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus.
b) No, these organisms cannot complete their lifecycle in humans (cannot access the GI tract) and thus no systemic disease is possible.
c) Treatment for hookworm - albendazole or ivermectin x 1 dose.

questions.question: 15. Strongyloidiasis

parts.text: a) Why is there a concern to treat with ivermectin if from a filaria endemic region (East/West Africa)?

cohort_answer.text: If patient has Loa Loa, ivermectin may precipitate encephalopathy (Loa Loa needs to be treated with DEC). Dx with serology or smear. Loa Loa: filarial nematode causing subcutaneous filariasis, vector = chrysops silacea and dimidiata (deerflies, bite during day). Takes ~5 months for larvae to become adult worms. Majority asymptomatic; symptoms - Calabar swellings and eye worm.

questions.question: Stool positive for B. hominis, Entamoeba hartmanni, Strongyloides, Trichuris trichiura eggs all in an asymptomatic patient 3 weeks after return from travel (self-limited diarrheal illness previously) – asked if you would treat each pathogen independently as yes/no and with what agent if you did.

parts.text: Complete pathogenicity/treat/treatment table for Strongyloides, E. hartmanni, Blastocystis hominis, Trichuris
b) Husband had self-limited diarrhea illness and is now well. Stool is positive for E. histolytica/dispar. What other test is needed?
c) Test is positive for E. histolytica. What would you treat with?

cohort_answer.text:
Strongyloides: pathogenic, yes treat (chronic strongy) until larvae no longer detected: Ivermectin 200mcg/kg x2 days 2 weeks apart (cure 94-100%) or Albendazole 400mg BID x3-5d (cure 38-87%). E. hartmanni: commensal, no treatment. Blastocystis hominis: rarely pathogenic, generally no treatment; if treated, Flagyl x10d or Septra x7d. Trichuris: proportional to pathogen amount, yes treat: Mebendazole 100mg PO BID x3d, Albendazole 400mg PO qd x3d, or Ivermectin 200ug/kg PO qd x3d
Antigen test for Gal/GalNAc-lectin to differentiate species; or PCR (microscopy cannot distinguish)
Asymptomatic cyst passer: Paromomycin 25-35mg/kg/day divided TID x7 days ("luminal chaser") OR Iodoquinol 650 TID x21d. If symptomatic diarrhea, would need metronidazole 500 TID x7 days plus paromomycin or iodoquinol after; since asymptomatic might forego that

questions.question: Patient from South America with E. coli meningitis and rapidly migrating perianal rash.

parts.text: What is the underlying infectious condition?
Name 3 ways to diagnose infection
What are two infections that predispose to Strongyloides?
What are two non-infectious conditions that predispose to this condition?

cohort_answer.text: Disseminated Strongyloidiasis (hyperinfection). Diagnosis: Serology; culture stool on agar plate (observe larvae migration); microscopy (stool O&P, duodenal aspirate, BAL, stool NAAT, perianal skin biopsy). Predisposing infections: HTLV-1, HIV. Non-infectious predisposing conditions: corticosteroid use, HSCT GvHD, TNF-alpha inhibition, hematologic malignancies, impaired gut motility, hypochlorhydria, DM, debilitating chronic diseases

questions.question: Recurrent Pinworm infection in an 8-year-old boy. Responds to treatment but symptoms return. Brother also had it recently

parts.text: Name genus and species
2 specific things regarding treatment
How do you launder (what and how)?
2 non-treatment things to tell family

cohort_answer.text: Genus/species: Enterobius vermicularis. Treatment: need to repeat 2 weeks later (doesn't kill larval form/eggs); need to treat entire household at same time. Laundering: all bedding and clothes, should not be shaken but carefully placed in wash in hot water followed by hot dryer to kill eggs. Non-treatment advice: shower daily to remove eggs off skin, cut fingernails daily and avoid biting them, hand hygiene is most effective prevention method.

questions.question: Complete the table: Organism | Nematode, Cestode, or Trematode | 1st Line Treatment, for Strongyloides, Fasciola, Schistosomiasis, Trichuris, Dibothriocephalus latum

parts.text: Complete table for Strongyloides, Fasciola, Schistosomiasis, Trichuris, Dibothriocephalus latum

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides - Nematode - Ivermectin. Fasciola - Trematode - Triclabendazole. Schistosomiasis - Trematode - Praziquantel. Trichuris - Nematode - Albendazole. Dibothriocephalus latus - Cestode - Praziquantel. Rule: all nematodes use albendazole except Strongyloides (Ivermectin); all cestodes/trematodes use praziquantel except Fasciola (Triclabendazole).

parts.text: Strongyloides, E hartmanni, blasto, trichuris Q - would you treat and with what?

questions.model_answer: Strongyloides stercoralis - treat (always, even if asymptomatic): ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day x2 days. E. hartmanni - do not treat (nonpathogenic commensal). Blastocystis hominis - do not treat if asymptomatic. Trichuris trichiura - treat: albendazole 400 mg daily x3 days.

questions.question: Woman recently traveled to rural ?cameroon and returned with diarrhea now resolved. A stool o and P is done

parts.text: indicate which of the following should be treated: Strongy, trichuria trichuris, dientamoeba fragilis, entaemoba hartmanii and with what?
husband found to have entaeomba histolytica/dispar in stool, what is one step you would do next, how would it help you?

questions.model_answer:
a) Treatment: Strongyloides stercoralis - treat with ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day x2 days. Trichuris trichiura - treat with albendazole 400 mg daily x3 days (or mebendazole). Dientamoeba fragilis - treat only if symptomatic, with metronidazole (or paromomycin/iodoquinol); this patient's diarrhea has resolved and stool shows it incidentally, so treatment is optional/can be deferred if truly asymptomatic. Entamoeba hartmanni - do not treat (nonpathogenic commensal).
b) Husband with E. histolytica/dispar on stool: send a stool antigen test (or PCR) specific for E. histolytica - this distinguishes the pathogenic E. histolytica (which requires treatment for invasive potential) from the morphologically identical but nonpathogenic E. dispar.

questions.question: Patient from endemic area with stongyloides in stool otherwise well.

parts.text: What is risk of treatment in patient if from region with endemic filariasis? 2 management strategies for patient about to undergo chemotherapy, with epidemiologic risk for strongyloides?

questions.model_answer:
a) Risk of ivermectin treatment in a patient from a region with endemic filariasis (particularly Loa loa in Central/West Africa): high-burden Loa loa microfilaremia can develop severe adverse reactions to ivermectin, including a Mazzotti-like reaction and, rarely, life-threatening encephalopathy, so co-infection should be screened for/considered before treating.
b) Two management strategies before chemotherapy in a patient with epidemiologic risk for strongyloidiasis: (1) screen with Strongyloides serology (and/or stool O&P) before starting immunosuppressive chemotherapy (2) if positive (or if screening is unavailable and risk is high), treat empirically with ivermectin (2 doses, 2 weeks apart) prior to initiating chemotherapy to prevent hyperinfection/dissemination syndrome.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3437-3441 (Strongyloides hyperinfection risk with immunosuppression)
questions.beyond_mandell: Loa loa/ivermectin encephalopathy risk is standard tropical medicine knowledge, not detailed in this nematode chapter excerpt.

questions.question: CLL:

parts.text: What type of immunodeficiency results
Name 2 parasites that cause weight loss and chronic diarrhea in these patients
Name 4 immunodeficiencies that cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections

cohort_answer.text: A) Humoral immunodeficiency-hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG3/4 most affected, IgA sometimes); cell-mediated immunodeficiency-reduced T cell function; complement deficiency-decreased properdin and B cell complement receptors; innate immunodeficiency-decreased neutrophil counts, decreased phagocytic activity. B) Giardia lamblia (with IgA def or hypogammaglobulinemia); Cryptosporidium (also with hypogammaglobulinemia). C) CVID, SCID, CGD, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, congenital neutropenia, complement deficiency, Wiskott Aldrich, DiGeorge syndrome (also CF, ciliary motility disorders, anatomic abnormalities, nephrotic syndrome).

questions.question: Woman returns from travel, had diarrhea a few weeks ago but now completely asymptomatic.

parts.text: Which of the following stool results do you treat (just a list; no pictures) and with what (write only ONE agent)? Strongyloides with filariform larvae, B hominis, E. hartmanii, Trichuris trichiura
Her boyfriend also develops diarrhea. Stool specimen reports says E. histolytica/dispar. What test do you do now and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) Treat: Strongyloides with filariform larvae - ivermectin. Trichuris trichiura - albendazole. Do not treat: B. hominis, E. hartmannii (both nonpathogenic commensals in an asymptomatic host).
b) Boyfriend's stool reports E. histolytica/dispar: order a stool antigen test (or PCR) specific for E. histolytica, because it distinguishes the pathogenic E. histolytica from the morphologically indistinguishable nonpathogenic E. dispar, and only E. histolytica requires treatment.

questions.question: Cutaneous larva migrans picture. The patient was from some South American country.

parts.text: What are two causative organisms. Both genus and species names required.
The GP wants to know if they have to worry about systemic disease. Yes or no and why
Treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, and Uncinaria stenocephala. Systemic disease: No - humans are dead-end host, can defer specific treatment since larvae won't progress through life cycle and will die, often regressing over weeks to months; often self-limited; migration may continue for months with severe pruritus interfering with sleep; hookworms unable to penetrate basal membrane to enter lymphatics so unable to complete life cycle and die without reproducing; rarely larvae found in sputum or cause visceral disease; main complication is secondary infection. (Distinction from larva currens/strongyloides: CLM migrates 1-2cm/day, larva currens 5-15cm/hr; rarely can have Loffler's syndrome from strongyloides.) Treatment: ivermectin 200mcg/kg/d x1-2 days or albendazole 400mg/d x3 days.

questions.question: Geohelminths.

parts.text: Definition?
Name 3 other than Strongy
What 2 public health concerns do they cause in endemic areas
2 public health strategies for control
Syndrome in developed countries/non-endemic regions related to them

cohort_answer.text: Definition: eggs or larvae mature on soil before becoming infective (soil-transmitted helminths, strictly depending on soil environment for a critical developmental stage of life cycle). Most common: Roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides); Whipworm (Trichuris trichiura); Hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale). Other than Strongy: Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura; Necator americanus; Ancylostoma duodenale. Public health concerns: Iron deficiency anemia (worms feed on host tissues/blood, hookworms cause chronic intestinal blood loss); Malnutrition (increased malabsorption, loss of appetite, roundworms compete for vitamin A); Diarrhea (particularly T. trichiura); Bowel prolapse; Dermatitis; Eosinophilia. Control strategies: Mass drug administration; Improving sanitation; Public knowledge/risk mitigation; Health and hygiene education. Syndrome in developed countries: Asymptomatic eosinophilia; Loeffler's syndrome (eosinophilic pneumonitis - transpulmonary passage of helminth larvae from Ascaris, hookworms, Strongyloides stercoralis; syndrome of transient pulmonary radiographic opacities and peripheral blood eosinophilia; mostly in travelers with first exposure); Strongyloides hyperinfection.

parts.text: Which soil-transmitted helminth has an oral ingestion but tissue migratory phase?
Draw the life cycle for this one

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides. Life cycle: adult worms live in lumen of small intestine; female produces ~200,000 eggs/day passed with feces; unfertilized eggs not infective; larvae develop to infectivity within fertile eggs after 18 days to several weeks depending on environment (optimum moist, warm, shaded soil); after infective eggs swallowed, larvae hatch, invade intestinal mucosa, carried via portal then systemic circulation to lungs; mature in lungs (10-14 days), penetrate alveolar walls, ascend bronchial tree to throat, swallowed; develop into adult worms in small intestine; 2-3 months from ingestion of infective eggs to oviposition; adult worms live 1-2 years. (Autoinfection examples: Strongyloides, Paracapillaria, Hymenolepis.)

questions.question: A patient has eosinophilia with no symptoms. A single stool O&P is performed and is negative.

parts.text: Name three possible infections
Give two reasons why single O&P not good enough for diagnosis.
Regarding strongyloides, what potential life-threatening infection could you avoid by treating for the above?

cohort_answer.text: Possible infections: Strongyloides; Schistosomiasis; HIV; Toxocara canis/cati; Hookworm; Hymenolepis nana; Clonorchis; Fasciola; Loiasis. Reasons single O&P insufficient: single stool sample insensitive for many parasites (intermittent shedding); parasite may not be excreted in stool. Life-threatening infection to avoid: hyperinfection syndrome with disseminated strongyloides, mainly in immunocompromised patients.

questions.question: Treatment for these 3 parasites.

parts.text: Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis)
Hymenolepis nana
[can't recall]

cohort_answer.text: Pinworm: mebendazole or albendazole or pyrantel pamoate. Hymenolepis nana: praziquantel. Third parasite: not recalled in source.

parts.text: List three nematodes with a lung phase

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides stercoralis; Ascaris lumbricoides; Ancylostoma duodenale; Necator americanus; Wuchereria bancrofti; Brugia malayi.

questions.question: Q4 (2013 PM). Patient with cutaneous larva migrans/larva currens picture.

parts.text: What are 2 causative organisms? Both genus and species names required
GP wants to know if they have to worry about systemic disease. Yes or no and why?
Treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Organisms: Cutaneous larva migrans (Ancylostoma caninum, A. braziliense, and Uncinaria stenocephala); Larva currens (Strongyloides stercoralis). Systemic disease: No - larvae of most species cannot mature within the human host since humans are incidental intermediate hosts; larvae migrate in epidermis and lack collagenase to break through basement membrane, producing an inflammatory reaction along the cutaneous tract lasting weeks; incubation several days up to months. Treatment: 1st line Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg once daily PO x1-2 days (2 days if folliculitis); 2nd line Albendazole 400mg daily with fatty meal x3 days (7 days if extensive disease).

questions.question: Q5 (2003 PM). Woman in Jamaica, on the beach. Cuts foot, gets rash on the sole, which moves to her ankle. Pruritis, otherwise systemically well.

parts.text: Diagnosis?

cohort_answer.text: Cutaneous larva migrans.

questions.question: Q9 (2015). Woman recently traveled to rural Cameroon and returned with diarrhea which has now resolved.

parts.text: A) Stool O+P is done - indicate which of the following should be treated and with what? Organism | Treatment: Strongyloides stercoralis; Trichuris trichiura; Dientamoeba fragilis; Entamoeba hartmanii
B) Husband found to have entamoeba histolytica/dispar in stool. What is one step you would do next, how would it help you?

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis - Yes: Ivermectin 200 ug/kg for 2 days or 1 dose repeated 2 weeks after (screen for hypermicrofilaremia with loa loa prior to treatment); Trichuris trichiura - Yes: Mebendazole 500mg PO daily x3 days (superior to albendazole); Dientamoeba fragilis - No; Entamoeba hartmanii - No (non-pathogenic amebae). B) E. histolytica confirmed by trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes or positive immunoassay AND PCR; PCR differentiates histolytica from dispar - gold standard, 100x more sensitive than antigen assay, up to 100% specific; facilitates early diagnosis and can follow treatment response.

questions.question: Q79 (2012 AM). Strongyloides with filarial co-infection.

parts.text: A) What is the risk of ivermectin?
B) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for strongyloides going to start immunosuppression?

cohort_answer.text: A) Administration of ivermectin to highly loa loa microfilaremic subjects can precipitate life-threatening encephalopathy. Relative contraindications: confirmed/suspected loa loa infection (albendazole alternative), previous hypersensitivity, weight<15kg or age<1 year, pregnant women (category C). B) 'Test and treat' approach; empiric administration of ivermectin to at-risk patients before immunosuppression before results are back.

questions.question: Q29 (2010 PM). Patient recently immigrated who has eosinophilia, but stool O+P negative. No real symptoms otherwise. Positive serology for Strongyloides and Schistosomiasis. Stool O+P negative

parts.text: A) Give 3 most common causes for asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient
B) Give 2 reasons why the stool O+P is negative

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides, Schistosomiasis, and hookworm are most commonly identified parasites (network +REDIVI data: S. stercoralis 34.4%, Schistosoma sp 11.0%, hookworm 8.6%). Other infectious causes: Filariae, HIV-1, various helminths. Non-infectious: allergy/atopic disease, drug reaction, hypoadrenalism, tumor-associated, hypereosinophilic syndromes. B) Stool O+P is very insensitive for Strongyloides (intermittent shedding) and Schistosomiasis; parasite not always excreted in stool (S. haematobium eggs excreted in urine not stool); for strongyloides eggs degrade before leaving body, need to look for rhabditiform larvae specifically; interval from acquisition to positive test result can be 3-4 weeks before GI symptoms/worms in intestine.

parts.text: A) Define/explain strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome
Give 2 treatments

cohort_answer.text: Hyperinfection syndrome occurs when low cellular immunity leads to strongyloides dissemination with extra-intestinal involvement, typically due to steroids or concurrent HTLV infection; accelerated autoinfection with higher parasite quantity in typical autoinfection cycle locations; often associated with gram negative sepsis. Disseminated strongyloidiasis = hyperinfection with spread to organs/tissues outside autoinfection cycle (skin, lungs, GI); both diagnosed by finding parasite in fluid outside GI tract. Treatment: Ivermectin 200ug/kg/d x2 weeks minimum PLUS Albendazole 400mg PO BID x7 days.

questions.question: Q52 (2010 PM). Woman immigrated from India 6 years ago. Now has asymptomatic eosinophilia on 3 occasions for the past 3 months. IgE elevated. Normal LFTs, OB negative and stool O+P negative

parts.text: A) Name the top 3 diagnoses
B) List 3 investigations you would do next

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis; Schistosomiasis; HIV; Helminths (filariasis). B) HIV serology; Strongyloides serology; Schistosoma serology; Stool ova + parasite; Filarial serology.

questions.question: Q77 (2012 AM, 2011 PM, 2009 AM). Geohelminths

parts.text: A) Definition:
B) Apart from Strongyloides, name 3 others
C) What 2 public health concerns do they cause in endemic areas?
D) 2 public health strategies for control
E) Syndromes in developed countries/non-endemic regions

cohort_answer.text: A) Soil transmitted helminths - part of life cycle involves living in soil. B) Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura (whipworm); Necator americanus (hookworm); Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm). C) Anemia; Malnutrition; Stunting/poor growth/failure to thrive; Developmental delay. D) Mass drug administration; Improving sanitation; Public education (e.g. wearing shoes). E) Asymptomatic eosinophilia; Loeffler's syndrome (except Trichuris, no lung phase); Strongyloides hyperinfection; Trichuris prolapsed rectum; Ascaris bowel obstruction.

parts.text: Of the soil-transmitted helminths, which one has oral ingestion but tissue migratory phase?
Draw the life cycle for this one

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides.

questions.question: Q81 (2008). Treatment for these 3 parasites: Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis); Hymenolepsis nana; [third parasite not recalled by author]

parts.text: Give treatment for each parasite

cohort_answer.text: Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) - mebendazole. Hymenolepsis nana - praziquantel (cestode causing weakness, headaches, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhea). Third parasite: not recalled.

parts.text: List 3 nematodes with a lung phase

cohort_answer.text: Ascaris lumbricoides; Strongyloides stercoralis; Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus); Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi (tropical pulmonary eosinophilia). (Note: Paragonimiasis is NOT a nematode, it is a trematode.) Essentially any cause of Loeffler's syndrome has a lung phase.

questions.question: Choice of agent and whether to treat or not for: Strongyloides; Trichuris trichiura; Entamoeba hartmanii; Blastocystis (no symptoms). A patient's husband has Entamoeba histolytica/dispar in the stool. What test to differentiate the Entamoeba?

parts.text: Strongyloides - treat and with what?
Trichuris trichiura - treat and with what?
Entamoeba hartmanii - treat?
Blastocystis (no symptoms) - treat?
Test to differentiate E. histolytica/dispar

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides: Yes - Ivermectin 1-2 days (non-disseminated). Trichuris trichiura: Yes - Mebendazole x3 days (100mg orally BID x3 days, adults and children). Entamoeba hartmanii: No. Blastocystis (asymptomatic): No. Test: EIA allows E. histolytica differentiation. Treatment if E. histolytica confirmed: asymptomatic = intraluminal agent only (paromomycin x7d); diarrhea/extraintestinal = flagyl 750mg PO TID x7d then intraluminal agent (paromomycin x7d).
